edits.old: For big $\theta$, the family is uniformly bounded above. Indeed, choose $m$ such that $D=\{\varphi>-m\}$ has positive smooth volume $d$. On $D$, every competitor satisfies $h\leq L:=b\sup_Xu+(b-1)m$. Choose $C>0$ with $\theta\leq C\omega$. The normalized $L^1$ estimate \eqref{eq:normalized-lone}, applied after scaling, gives $\int_X|h-\sup_Xh|\,\mathrm{d}V\leq K$. Thus $\sup_Xh\leq L+K/d$ whenever $\sup_Xh>L$, and the bound is immediate otherwise. The local envelope theorem then shows that $Q_b$ is a genuine potential. The defining convex inequality holds everywhere by the canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives. These facts are also recorded in \cite[Propositions 2.4 and Lemma 2.5]{ALS26} and \cite[Section 2.1]{XL26}.
edits.new: When the family is nonempty, its envelope is a genuine potential. Indeed, the obstacle $bu-(b-1)\varphi$ is finite almost everywhere, so the finite-sublevel argument at the start of the chapter gives a common upper bound for the competitors. The local envelope theorem applies, and the defining convex inequality holds everywhere by the canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives. This argument needs no bigness or mass hypothesis. The construction in a semipositive big background is also recorded in \cite[Propositions 2.4 and Lemma 2.5]{ALS26}, and in an arbitrary big background in \cite[Section 2.1]{XL26}.

edits.old: Every mixed term in $T$ is semipositive, as is $\mathrm{d}w\wedge\dc w$. When $\ddc T=0$, the nonnegative smooth integrand on the left has zero integral and therefore vanishes everywhere. At any point with $f>0$, both $A$ and $B$ are positive definite. In particular, the term $B^{n-1}$ shows that $\mathrm{d}w\wedge\dc w\wedge T=0$ forces $\mathrm{d}w=0$ at that point. Density of $\{f>0\}$ and continuity of $\mathrm{d}w$ give $\mathrm{d}w=0$ on all of $X$. Connectedness proves the assertion.
edits.new: For the uniqueness conclusion, apply \cref{uni-thm:cofactor-intro}(1) with $h=1$. At every point with $f>0$, the form $B$ is positive definite, so the term $B^{n-1}$ makes the cofactor strictly positive. Its positivity locus is therefore dense, as required.

edits.old:
We first derive domination from ordinary bounded comparison.  Let
\(a,b\in\PSH(X,\omega)\cap L^\infty\) and suppose
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_\omega(a)(\{a<b\})=0.
\]
Add the same constant to both so that
\(b\leq0\).  For \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(0<t<1\) with
\(t\|b\|_\infty<\varepsilon\), and put
\(b_t=(1-t)b-\varepsilon\).  Then
\[
 \{a<b-2\varepsilon\}\subset\{a<b_t\}\subset\{a<b\},
 \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\omega(b_t)\geq t^n\omega^n.
\]
Comparison gives
\[
 t^n\int_{\{a<b-2\varepsilon\}}\omega^n
 \leq\int_{\{a<b_t\}}\mathrm{MA}_\omega(b_t)
 \leq\int_{\{a<b_t\}}\mathrm{MA}_\omega(a)=0.
\]
Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives \(a\geq b\) almost everywhere.
Local ball averages converge pointwise to each bounded quasi-psh
representative, so this ordering holds everywhere.
